## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet, and scores stay hidden for the whole search, so each round is a set of independent bets. Reasoning about the task: a placement is correct when, across the brick's footprint, every column's next target cell above the current build top sits at the same layer, and that layer equals the highest build top under the footprint. The baseline's per-column 1x1 stem with footprint max/min/avg pooling suits this well. The likely limits are the training budget (about 32 PPO updates of 4096 steps), the quality of the column encoder, and how much nonlinear capacity the head has. So the bets are: (A) the same network with fewer PPO epochs, which gives about 1.86x more fresh samples; (B) a richer column encoder and head that also sees global context; (C) a layer-wise column encoder that shares weights across layers and uses cumulative max over layers to learn the build heights and the next missing target layer.

### Round 2
No scores are shown, so I can only reason from the task. All three round-1 files trained without errors. To score a placement correctly, the network must find the landing layer z, which is the highest build cell under the footprint. It must then check three things: every footprint cell at layer z is a missing target cell, no missing target cell would be sealed below z, and no build cell sits at or above z. Every network so far flattens the layers into column features before pooling over the footprint. That makes the network learn comparisons across columns at the same layer, which is hard. I propose a head that pools over the footprint separately on each layer, using per-layer features learned with cumulative max up and down the column, and then takes a logsumexp over layers. All per-layer features come from learned layers. Two trials use this head with different recipes. One trial keeps the baseline network and uses a longer-horizon recipe (gamma 0.98, lambda 0.95, longer rollouts) to reward exact completion more. We cannot see seed noise here.

### Round 3
No scores are visible, only that all six trials trained without errors, so the choices here rest on the task's structure and not on measured results. A placement is right when the brick's landing layer, which is the highest filled cell under its footprint, matches the target exactly on that layer. That makes the per-layer footprint head (r2c1/r2c3) the best structural match: the landing-and-fit check stays local to one layer. Using fewer PPO epochs gives more fresh designs at the same compute, and fresh designs should help generalisation to held-out designs, so the 2-epoch runs are probably at least as good as the default 4. Since the final pick is the best 2-seed trial, it is worth covering different directions. Two candidates refine the per-layer head: one combines it with the whole-episode recipe (two recipe changes at once), and one uses a single epoch for the most data. The third adds global self-attention so each column gets whole-board context for build order.

### Round 4
Scores are hidden, so the analysis rests on how well each design fits the task. In this world a brick's fate depends on where it lands. The per-layer footprint head (r2c1) makes the "does it land at z and match the target" check local to one layer, so it is the strongest guess. All three trials ran without errors, and the 1-epoch run reached 315k steps within the time limit. This is the last round and selection takes the best trial, so I combine plausible gains instead of testing one change at a time. (1) 1 epoch plus whole-episode, longer-horizon rollouts: the most fresh designs, with credit for irreversible mistakes. (2) A shared 3x3 conv within each layer before the footprint pooling, so the head can see same-layer neighbours when choosing how to split a layer into bricks. (3) Column attention with 1 epoch, which recovers the samples lost to the attention block's extra compute.
